context.heading: Violence against a brother
context.body: Chamas ("violence") means ruthless wrongdoing, the word used for the corruption that brought the flood (Genesis 6:11). What makes Edom's violence worse is the relationship: Esau and Jacob were twins (Genesis 25). Moses' law even told Israel not to despise an Edomite, because "he is your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:7).

context.heading: Eight things you should not have done
context.body: Verses 12–14 build a ladder of "do not": do not gloat, rejoice, boast, enter the gate, look down, loot, stand at the crossroads to cut off fugitives, or hand over survivors. Most scholars connect this with Babylon's capture of Jerusalem in 586 BC (Psalm 137:7; Lamentations 4:21–22). Some date it to an earlier raid on Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 21:16–17).

context.heading: What goes around
context.body: Gemul ("recompense") means what someone has earned, a payback. "As you have done, it will be done to you" (v. 15). Edom's own deeds will boomerang back on its head. Verses 1–9 also closely parallel Jeremiah 49:7–16, showing this verdict on Edom was well known among the prophets.

theology.title: The kingdom will be the LORD's
theology.body: The book's last line sets everything in place: not Edom, not Babylon, not even Israel, but the LORD will reign (v. 21). Revelation 11:15 echoes it: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ."

theology.title: The long story of two brothers
theology.body: The rivalry between Jacob and Esau runs from Genesis through Malachi 1:2–4. Later the Edomites, pushed west by the Nabateans, settled in southern Judah as the Idumeans. Herod the Great came from an Idumean family, and he tried to kill the infant Jesus. Paul uses Jacob and Esau in Romans 9:10–13 to show God's free choice of mercy.

application.title: You stood aloof
application.body: Edom's first sin was not attacking but watching from a distance while strangers looted (v. 11). Bystanders are not neutral when they could help.
application.question: Where are you watching someone get hurt and telling yourself it is not your business?

application.title: The joy of someone's downfall
application.body: Gloating over a rival's fall, especially online, feels harmless. Obadiah says God takes it personally.
application.question: Whose failure have you secretly enjoyed, and what would it look like to pray for them instead?

application.title: Family wounds
application.body: Edom and Israel nursed a family grudge for centuries. Bitterness between relatives can outlast the original offense by generations.
application.question: What family grudge are you keeping alive that God may be asking you to lay down?
